caveats.statement: Freeze tolerance varies among populations and protocols; Alaska-specific laboratory results are not universal species limits.
Do not use “frozen solid” without qualification: survivable freezing is dominated by extracellular and extra-organ ice, while intracellular ice is dangerous.
Heartbeat, pulmonary ventilation and circulation are separate claims. The reviewed evidence directly measures cardiac activity and ventilation; direct zero-flow evidence was not located.

claims.statement: Wood frogs can survive nonlethal freezing in which up to about two-thirds of total body water becomes extracellular ice.

caveats: The study documents a reversible physiological arrest during controlled nonlethal freezing; it does not mean the frog died.

claims.statement: During controlled nonlethal freezing, cardiac activity in wood frogs can cease near the completion of ice formation.

claims.statement: After freezing begins, liver glycogen is rapidly converted to glucose and distributed as a cryoprotectant that reduces body ice and cellular injury.

caveats: Do not depict urea as a simultaneous liver-to-tissue surge equivalent to glucose; timing and tissue distribution differ.

hooks.text: A wood frog can survive a freeze that stops its heartbeat—then thaw and recover.
hooks.viewerPromise: Explain how extracellular ice and cryoprotectants make reversible physiological arrest survivable.

hooks.text: Much of a wood frog’s body water can freeze—but the ice forms mainly outside its cells.
hooks.viewerPromise: Replace the misleading “frozen solid” image with the real water-and-ice mechanism.

hooks.text: How does a frog protect its cells when much of its body water turns to ice?
hooks.viewerPromise: Reveal how extracellular ice, glucose and urea work together without implying that cells freeze internally.

thesis: Wood frogs survive nonlethal whole-body freezing by keeping ice mainly outside cells, redistributing water, and using glucose and urea as complementary cryoprotectants.
viewerPayoff: The frog does not become uniformly frozen inside every cell: it survives by managing extracellular ice, cellular dehydration, and the order in which protective chemistry and physiology change.
